title: CONDITIONAL SENTENCES
notes:
✓ Conditional sentence → a sentence that expresses a condition and its possible result.

✓ Most conditional sentences contain two clauses → the if-clause (condition) + the main clause (result).

✓ If it rains, we will stay home.

✓ Condition → If it rains.
✓ Result → we will stay home.

✓ The if-clause can come first or second.
If you study hard, you will pass.
You will pass if you study hard.

✓ When the if-clause comes first, normally use a comma before the main clause.

title: TYPES OF CONDITIONALS
notes:
◆ ZERO CONDITIONAL → general truths, facts, rules, and predictable results.
◆ FIRST CONDITIONAL → real or possible future situations.
◆ SECOND CONDITIONAL → hypothetical, unlikely, or unreal present/future situations.
◆ THIRD CONDITIONAL → unreal or impossible past situations and their imagined results.
◆ MIXED CONDITIONAL → combines different time references, usually past condition + present result or present condition + past result.

◆ QUICK MEMORY
Zero = fact
First = possible
Second = hypothetical
Third = impossible past
Mixed = different time relationship.

title: ZERO CONDITIONAL
notes:
◆ STRUCTURE
If + Present Simple, Present Simple.

✓ If you heat water, it boils.
✓ If people do not eat, they become hungry.

✓ Uses → scientific facts, general truths, natural laws, routines, rules, instructions, and situations that are generally or always true.

✓ Other connectors → when, whenever.
✓ When water reaches 100°C, it boils.
✓ Whenever I drink coffee at night, I cannot sleep.

✓ Both clauses normally use Present Simple because the result is presented as generally true.

title: FIRST CONDITIONAL
notes:
◆ STRUCTURE
If + Present Simple, will + V1.

✓ If I study hard, I will pass the exam.
✓ If it rains, we will stay home.

✓ Use → real, possible, or likely future conditions and their consequences.

✓ Negative → If + Present Simple, will not + V1.
✓ If you do not hurry, you will miss the bus.

✓ The result clause can also come first.
✓ You will miss the bus if you do not hurry.

✓ Do not normally use will in the if-clause.
❌ If it will rain, we will stay home.
✓ If it rains, we will stay home.

title: FIRST CONDITIONAL: VARIATIONS
notes:
✓ The result clause does not always require will.

✓ If you study, you may pass. → possibility.
✓ If you study, you can pass. → ability/possibility.
✓ If you study, you should pass. → expected result/advice.
✓ If you study, you must pass. → strong requirement/consequence.
✓ If you study, you might pass. → weaker possibility.

✓ Imperative result → If you see John, tell him to call me.

✓ Present Simple result for scheduled/automatic outcomes → If you press this button, the machine starts.

✓ Key point → the condition clause normally remains in Present Simple even when the result uses a modal or imperative.

title: SECOND CONDITIONAL
notes:
◆ STRUCTURE
If + Past Simple, would + V1.

✓ If I had more money, I would travel around the world.
✓ If she studied harder, she would pass.

✓ Uses → hypothetical situations, unlikely future possibilities, imaginary situations, advice, and situations contrary to present reality.

✓ If I were rich, I would build a school. → I am not rich.
✓ If I lived near the university, I would walk there. → I do not live near it.

✓ The Past Simple here does not necessarily mean past time. It can express distance from reality.

title: WERE IN THE SECOND CONDITIONAL
notes:
✓ In formal English, were is traditionally used with all subjects in hypothetical clauses.

✓ If I were you, I would apologize.
✓ If he were here, he would help us.
✓ If she were richer, she would travel more.

✓ In informal speech, was is sometimes used with I/he/she/it, but were is preferred in formal writing and examinations.

◆ IMPORTANT EXPRESSION
If I were you → used to give advice.

✓ If I were you, I would study more carefully.

title: THIRD CONDITIONAL
notes:
◆ STRUCTURE
If + Past Perfect, would have + V3.

✓ If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam.

✓ Use → imaginary or unreal situations in the past and their imagined consequences.

✓ If she had left earlier, she would have caught the bus.

→ She did not leave earlier, so she did not catch the bus.

✓ Negative → If + had not + V3, would have + V3.
✓ If I had not missed the bus, I would have arrived on time.

✓ Do not use would have in the if-clause in standard conditional structures.
❌ If I would have studied...
✓ If I had studied...

title: MIXED CONDITIONALS
notes:
✓ Mixed conditional → combines different time references between the condition and result.

◆ TYPE 1 → Past condition + Present result.

✓ Structure → If + Past Perfect, would + V1.
✓ If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.

→ I did not study medicine in the past, so my present situation is different.

◆ TYPE 2 → Present condition + Past result.

✓ Structure → If + Past Simple, would have + V3.
✓ If I were more careful, I would not have made that mistake.

→ My present characteristic caused a past consequence.

✓ Mixed conditionals are used when the condition and result belong to different times.

title: UNLESS
notes:
✓ Unless → means 'if not' and introduces a negative condition.

✓ Unless you study, you will fail.
= If you do not study, you will fail.

✓ Unless it rains, we will go outside.
= If it does not rain, we will go outside.

✓ Do not normally use another negative after unless.
❌ Unless you don't study, you will fail.
✓ Unless you study, you will fail.

✓ Unless is usually used when the condition is an exception to a result.

title: PROVIDED / PROVIDING / AS LONG AS
notes:
✓ Provided that / Providing that / As long as → express a condition or requirement.

✓ You can borrow my car provided that you drive carefully.
✓ You can come with us as long as you finish your work.
✓ We will support the project providing that it remains within budget.

✓ Meaning → the result is possible only if the stated condition is satisfied.

✓ These expressions are especially useful in formal English.

title: ON CONDITION THAT
notes:
✓ On condition that → means 'only if a particular condition is satisfied.'

✓ You may use the laboratory on condition that you follow the safety rules.
✓ He agreed to help on condition that we kept the information confidential.

✓ Common in formal agreements, rules, and conditions.

title: IN CASE
notes:
✓ In case → expresses a precaution against a possible future situation.

✓ Take an umbrella in case it rains.
✓ Save the document in case the computer crashes.

✓ In case does NOT mean exactly the same as if.

✓ If it rains, we will stay home. → condition.
✓ Take an umbrella in case it rains. → precaution.

✓ In case means 'because something might happen.'

title: EVEN IF / EVEN THOUGH
notes:
✓ Even if → introduces a hypothetical condition that will not change the result.
✓ Even if it rains, we will play the match.

✓ Even though → introduces a real fact or situation that contrasts with another fact.
✓ Even though it was raining, we played the match.

✓ Difference → even if = hypothetical; even though = known/real fact.

title: WHETHER ... OR NOT
notes:
✓ Whether ... or not → expresses that the result is the same regardless of the condition.

✓ Whether you agree or not, we will continue.
✓ I will go whether it rains or not.

✓ Meaning → the condition does not affect the final result.

title: ONLY IF / IF AND ONLY IF
notes:
✓ Only if → emphasizes that a condition is necessary.
✓ You can enter only if you have a ticket.

✓ If and only if → expresses a two-way necessary-and-sufficient relationship, especially in formal or logical contexts.
✓ A number is divisible by 2 if and only if it is even.

✓ Only if can create inversion when placed at the beginning.
✓ Only if you work hard will you succeed.

title: ALTERNATIVES TO IF
notes:
◆ COMMON CONDITIONAL EXPRESSIONS
✓ unless → if not
✓ provided that → if this condition is satisfied
✓ providing that → if this condition is satisfied
✓ as long as → if a condition continues to be true
✓ on condition that → only if
✓ in case → as a precaution
✓ supposing/suppose → imagine if
✓ assuming that → if we accept this condition
✓ whether or not → regardless of the condition
✓ only if → only under this condition

✓ Suppose you won the lottery. What would you do?
✓ Assuming that he agrees, we can start tomorrow.

title: SUPPOSE / SUPPOSING
notes:
✓ Suppose / Supposing → introduces an imagined or hypothetical situation.

✓ Suppose you lost your phone. What would you do?
✓ Supposing we missed the train, where would we stay?

✓ Often used with Second Conditional meaning for hypothetical situations.
✓ Suppose I were you, I would accept the offer.

title: IF + SHOULD
notes:
✓ If + should → expresses a possible but relatively unlikely future event, often in formal English.

✓ If you should need help, call me.
✓ If he should arrive early, tell him to wait.

✓ Meaning is close to → If you happen to need help...

✓ It is more formal than the ordinary First Conditional.

title: IF + HAPPEN TO
notes:
✓ If + happen to + V1 → emphasizes that an event may occur by chance.

✓ If you happen to see Sarah, give her this message.
✓ If you happen to need anything, let me know.

✓ It suggests an accidental or uncertain possibility.

title: UNREAL PAST: WISH AND IF ONLY
notes:
✓ Wish + Past Simple → regret or dissatisfaction about the present.

✓ I wish I had more money.
= I do not have enough money now.

✓ Wish + Past Perfect → regret about the past.

✓ I wish I had studied harder.
= I did not study hard enough.

✓ Wish + would → desire for a change in another person's behavior or an annoying situation.

✓ I wish you would stop shouting.

✓ If only → stronger form of wish.
✓ If only I were richer!
✓ If only I had studied harder!

✓ Wish and if only express unreal or desired situations rather than ordinary conditional results.

title: CONDITIONALS WITH MODAL VERBS
notes:
✓ The result clause can use modal verbs other than will/would.

✓ If you finish early, you can leave.
→ permission/ability.

✓ If you study hard, you may pass.
→ possibility.

✓ If you are tired, you should rest.
→ advice.

✓ If you want to succeed, you must work hard.
→ necessity.

✓ If he had asked me, I could have helped him.
→ past ability/possibility.

✓ Modal choice changes the meaning of the result.

title: CONDITIONALS AND TIME
notes:
◆ ZERO
Present condition + Present result.
✓ If you heat ice, it melts.

◆ FIRST
Present condition + Future possibility.
✓ If you study, you will pass.

◆ SECOND
Past-form condition + Hypothetical present/future result.
✓ If I had money, I would travel.

◆ THIRD
Past Perfect condition + Imagined past result.
✓ If I had studied, I would have passed.

◆ MIXED
Condition and result refer to different times.
✓ If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.

title: CONDITIONAL INVERSION
notes:
✓ In formal English, some if-clauses can be inverted by removing if.

✓ If I were you → Were I you.
✓ If he were here → Were he here.

✓ If you should need help → Should you need help.
✓ If you should have any questions → Should you have any questions.

✓ If I had known → Had I known.
✓ If they had arrived earlier → Had they arrived earlier.

◆ COMMON PATTERNS
Were + subject
Should + subject
Had + subject + V3

✓ Had I known about the problem, I would have helped.

✓ This structure is formal and is common in formal writing and examinations.

title: CONDITIONAL INVERSION: MEANING
notes:
✓ Had I known = If I had known.
✓ Were I richer = If I were richer.
✓ Should you need assistance = If you should need assistance.

✓ The meaning remains conditional, but the structure becomes more formal and concise.

✓ Do not use inversion with ordinary Present Simple if-clauses.
❌ Do you study hard, you will pass.
✓ If you study hard, you will pass.

title: CONDITIONALS WITH IMPERATIVES
notes:
✓ A conditional sentence can have an imperative in the result clause.

✓ If you see John, tell him to call me.
✓ If you finish your work, come outside.
✓ If you feel sick, see a doctor.

✓ The condition determines when the instruction should be followed.

✓ The imperative does not require will.

title: IF-CLAUSE POSITION
notes:
✓ Condition first → comma is normally used.
✓ If you study hard, you will pass.

✓ Result first → comma is normally not used.
✓ You will pass if you study hard.

✓ The meaning remains the same.

✓ With long or complicated clauses, punctuation may vary according to sentence structure, but the standard school rule is → comma after an initial if-clause.

title: COMMON CONDITIONAL MISTAKES
notes:
❌ If it will rain, we will stay home.
✓ If it rains, we will stay home.

❌ If I would have money, I would travel.
✓ If I had money, I would travel.

❌ If I would have studied, I would have passed.
✓ If I had studied, I would have passed.

❌ Unless you don't study, you will fail.
✓ Unless you study, you will fail.

❌ If I was you, I would apologize. (formal exam English)
✓ If I were you, I would apologize.

❌ If I had studied, I would pass yesterday.
✓ If I had studied, I would have passed yesterday.

❌ If you will arrive early, call me.
✓ If you arrive early, call me.

❌ If I knew the answer yesterday, I would tell you.
✓ If I had known the answer yesterday, I would have told you.

✓ Main exam trap → identify the time of the condition and the time of the result before choosing the tense.

title: CONDITIONALS MASTER FORMULA
notes:
◆ ZERO
If + Present Simple → Present Simple
✓ If you heat ice, it melts.

◆ FIRST
If + Present Simple → will + V1
✓ If I study, I will pass.

◆ SECOND
If + Past Simple → would + V1
✓ If I studied, I would pass.

◆ THIRD
If + Past Perfect → would have + V3
✓ If I had studied, I would have passed.

◆ MIXED 1
If + Past Perfect → would + V1
✓ If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.

◆ MIXED 2
If + Past Simple → would have + V3
✓ If I were more careful, I would not have made that mistake.

title: HOW TO IDENTIFY THE CONDITIONAL
notes:
✓ Is it a general truth or automatic result? → ZERO.

✓ Is the future condition realistic or possible? → FIRST.

✓ Is it imaginary, unlikely, or contrary to present reality? → SECOND.

✓ Is it about an unreal past event that cannot now be changed? → THIRD.

✓ Does the condition belong to one time and the result to another? → MIXED.

◆ QUICK TEST
FACT → Zero
POSSIBLE FUTURE → First
IMAGINARY PRESENT/FUTURE → Second
IMAGINARY PAST → Third
PAST ↔ PRESENT CONNECTION → Mixed.

title: CONDITIONAL SENTENCE EXAM STRATEGY
notes:
◆ 1. Find the condition marker → if, unless, provided, as long as, etc.
◆ 2. Determine whether the condition is real, possible, hypothetical, or impossible.
◆ 3. Determine the time → general, present/future, past, or mixed.
◆ 4. Select the appropriate conditional pattern.
◆ 5. Check the verb after IF.
◆ 6. Check the result clause and modal verb.
◆ 7. Check whether a negative form changes the meaning.
◆ 8. Check whether the sentence expresses a fact, possibility, advice, regret, or hypothetical situation.

◆ REMEMBER
Zero → If + Present, Present.
First → If + Present, will + V1.
Second → If + Past, would + V1.
Third → If + Past Perfect, would have + V3.
Mixed → different time references.

✓ Golden Rule → In ordinary conditional sentences, do not automatically put WILL or WOULD immediately after IF. First identify the conditional type and meaning.
